explanation:
## The program

```cpp
int divisorSum(int n)
{
    int total{};
    for (int d = 1; d < n; ++d)
        if (n % d == 0) total += d;
    return total;
}

bool isPerfect(int n)
{
    return n == divisorSum(n);
}
```

## A one-line function earns its place

`isPerfect` does nothing a reader could not have written inline.
What it does is put a name on the comparison, so that the loop in
`main` says what it is looking for:

```cpp
if (isPerfect(k))                 // reads as the definition
if (k == divisorSum(k))           // reads as an implementation
```

Both compile to the same thing. The first survives the day somebody
wants abundant numbers as well, because then there is an obvious
place to put `isAbundant`.

## Predicates are used directly

```cpp
if (isPerfect(k))              // yes
if (isPerfect(k) == true)      // the same thing, said twice
if (isPerfect(k) != false)     // and again
return n == divisorSum(n);     // yes
if (n == divisorSum(n)) return true; else return false;   // no
```

A function returning `bool` returns the condition itself. Comparing
a `bool` to `true` is the same reflex as writing `if (x == true)`,
and worth losing early.

## Proper divisors stop below n

`for (int d = 1; d < n; ++d)` — strictly less than. With `<=` every
number would include itself and the sum would always exceed it, so
nothing would ever be perfect and the program would print `none` for
every input. That is a satisfying bug to find, because the output is
uniform and gives no hint where to look.

`divisorSum(1)` is 0: the loop runs zero times. So 1 is not perfect,
which is correct and falls out rather than being special-cased.

## The flag, and what it is for

`found` records whether the loop printed anything, so that `none`
can be printed afterwards if it did not. The alternative — deciding
in advance whether the range contains a perfect number — means
doing the whole search twice.

This is a common shape: a loop that may produce nothing, and a
message for the empty case that can only be decided once the loop is
over.

## How slow is it, really

This is Ο(n²): for every `k` up to `n`, a loop up to `k`. At
n = 10,000 that is about 50 million remainder operations, which is
fast enough here and would not be at n = 1,000,000.

The standard improvement is to stop at √n and add both members of
each divisor pair, which turns Ο(n) per number into Ο(√n). It is
worth knowing and is not the exercise — and it is fiddly to get
right for perfect squares, where the pair is one number counted
once.

## What this does not check

Anything above 10,000, where the Ο(n²) loop starts to matter, and
the odd perfect numbers — none is known, and none is known not to
exist. Every perfect number ever found is even.
